turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, I’m your doctor today. What brings you in today? Patient: About two days ago while playing football, my right ring finger got caught in someone’s jersey and they pulled away forcefully. Since then it’s been progressively swollen and painful, and I can’t flex it at the distal interphalangeal joint when I make a fist.

[REASONING]
Key findings: 2 days after a traumatic pull injury to the right ring finger; progressive swelling and pain; inability to flex the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint when making a fist suggests possible extensor/flexor tendon injury—especially flexor tendon rupture at/near the insertion (flexor digitorum profundus, FDP).
Top candidates:
1) Rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its point of insertion — classic mechanism (forceful pull), swelling, and loss of active DIP flexion.
2) Other tendon injury (e.g., flexor tendon partial tear) — could also cause pain/swelling but usually some preserved motion.
3) Fracture/avulsion injury around the DIP — can limit motion and cause swelling; would expect focal bony tenderness or deformity.
4) Severe sprain/contusion — swelling and pain, but typically not complete loss of isolated DIP flexion.
5) Infection (less likely given acute traumatic onset) — would expect redness, warmth, fever, delayed onset.
Most informative next question: determine whether there is any active DIP flexion and compare with passive range of motion.
[/REASONING]
Can you actively bend (flex) the DIP joint at all against resistance, or is it completely unable to flex—also, if I move the finger for you (passive motion), does the DIP joint move normally?
Patient: I can’t flex the DIP joint at all when I try to make a fist, even against resistance. If you move it for me passively, the DIP joint does bend normally, but it’s very painful.

[REASONING]
Key findings updated: No active DIP flexion even against resistance; passive DIP flexion is possible but painful. This strongly supports an FDP tendon rupture (active loss with preserved passive motion).
Top candidates:
1) Rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its point of insertion — best fit: traumatic pull, inability to actively flex DIP, passive motion intact.
2) Flexor tendon laceration/partial rupture — would usually have some residual active flexion, but could be near-complete; still less likely than complete rupture.
3) Avulsion fracture involving the flexor insertion (bony mallet-type variants) — passive motion possible but pain; however complete loss of active DIP flexion after pull can mimic tendon rupture; needs exam/imaging.
4) Joint injury/volar plate injury — usually affects PIP more than isolated DIP flexion.
5) Infection is unlikely due to immediate traumatic onset.
Most informative next question: is there any visible deformity or “bowstringing,” and specifically is the fingertip resting in extension compared with the other hand (i.e., does the DIP droop)?
[/REASONING]
Does your right ring finger’s fingertip droop or rest more extended than the other ring finger (a noticeable “DIP droop”)?

Doctor: Does your right ring finger’s fingertip droop or rest more extended than the other ring finger—like a noticeable DIP droop? Patient: Yes, my right ring finger rests extended, and I can’t curl it at the fingertip when I try.

[REASONING]
Key findings: Traumatic pull injury; progressive swelling/pain; complete loss of active DIP flexion; passive DIP flexion possible but painful; fingertip rests extended with DIP droop. This is highly characteristic of FDP tendon rupture at the insertion (flexor digitorum profundus).
Top candidates:
1) Rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its point of insertion — strongest match (mechanism + complete loss of active DIP flexion + DIP droop + passive motion intact).
2) Flexor tendon laceration/rupture (partial) — less likely because you have complete active loss.
3) Avulsion fracture at the flexor insertion — can cause similar droop; would need x-ray to distinguish.
4) Less likely: joint/ligament injury causing functional limitation — would not typically produce classic tendon droop with preserved passive motion.
5) Infection — unlikely.
Most informative next step (to confirm and rule out fracture): obtain an x-ray of the finger to look for avulsion fracture and assess bony involvement.
[/REASONING]
